title: In ASASSN-14ko the soft X-ray switch-off comes 2.8 days before the UV flare (25 percent level, 2020-2023) and does not follow the UV flux, so the X-ray clock times the flare trigger
abstract: Question: campaign studies use the soft X-ray deep suppression of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko as an orbital clock (constant 108.44-d period in 2020-2024 while the published period decrease stopped). This needs the X-ray switch-off to be independent of the UV flare; if the flare quenched the corona (for example by Compton cooling), the dip would only be a second flare marker. Approach: we measured the UV state at the X-ray switch-off in every cycle with dense simultaneous data: Swift UVOT, XRT and NICER (cycles 20-33, from earlier SCI bundles) and, for cycle 30 (2023 August), the XMM-Newton Optical Monitor, which observed the nucleus in 23 visits at the same time as EPIC-pn. We measured the UV excess at the 30 percent X-ray crossing, the delays to 10, 25 and 50 percent of the peak UV excess (Monte Carlo over flux errors and the dip-time posterior), the X-ray level after the switch-off, and the luminosities. Results: at the switch-off the UVW2 excess is below 1 percent (cycle 20), 2.8 percent (cycle 21) and 7.4 percent (cycle 30, OM; 95 percent limits) of its peak, that is below 0.25-0.37 times the luminosity of the switching X-ray component (9.4e42 erg/s). The UV excess reaches 10, 25 and 50 percent of its peak 1.93 +/- 0.22, 2.80 +/- 0.09 and 3.62 +/- 0.13 d after the switch-off in cycles 20, 21, 22 and 30 (chi2 1.8-2.4 for 3 dof); the 2023 minus 2020-2021 change is -0.23 +/- 0.37 d. In 2020-2021 the X-rays came back near the UV peak, when the UV excess was 5.5-8.6 times the X-ray luminosity; in 2023-2024 they stayed low to the end of coverage (35-59 d). The median X-ray rate 3-60 d after the switch-off fell from 0.33-0.63 (six cycles) to 0.09-0.10 (three cycles; permutation p = 0.012). Conclusion: the X-ray switch-off is the first observed event of each flare and the X-ray level is not a function of the UV flux, so the X-ray clock times the flare trigger, not a radiative effect of the flare. The trigger-to-UV delay stayed constant while the period was constant and the X-ray response changed about five-fold. The trigger can be the star near pericentre or the leading returning debris; the data do not separate them. Limitations: three cycles give tight limits at the switch-off; extreme-UV photons are not observed; cycle 31 (gradual dip) gives a shorter delay (p = 0.05-0.13); eras were defined after inspection; pipeline products only.

display.caption: Six ASASSN-14ko cycles aligned on the X-ray deep suppression (dashed line). Top: soft X-ray level; bottom: UVW2 excess as a fraction of its peak (Swift UVOT; XMM OM in cycle 30). The UV flare starts after the X-ray switch-off in every cycle; the X-rays come back near the UV peak in 2020-2021 and stay low in 2023-2024.

Cycle 30 (2023 August) with XMM-Newton alone: EPIC-pn 0.5-2 keV flux above the floor (top) and simultaneous OM UVW2, UVM2 and UVW1 excess (bottom). The X-ray flux reaches its floor before the UV excess reaches 10 percent of its peak.

(a) Soft X-ray level against UVW2 excess: the X-rays switch off at zero UV excess and, in 2020-2021, return at the UV peak. (b) Order of events per cycle relative to the X-ray deep suppression: X-ray onset, deep suppression, UV 10/25/50 percent crossings, UVW2 peak, optical half-rise and X-ray recovery.

citations.reason: Its X-ray clock and its inference that the late flares are not a UV emission delay; we test the independence of the X-ray dip from the UV flare that this inference needs, and support it.
We use its f30 and f50 dip times, posterior draws and combined NICER/XRT visit rates.
We use its EPIC-pn time series, exponential switch-off fit and the spectral model of the switching component.
We use its optical half-rise times; our constant trigger-to-UV delay agrees with its constant half-rise lag.
We use its Swift UVOT per-observation photometry.
It shows that the switching X-ray source is the ASASSN-14ko nucleus and that the period did not react to X-ray state changes; we find a further change of the X-ray response with a constant clock.
Its precessing star-disc drag clock uses the X-ray dip as the pericentre; our result supports this use only if the trigger is the star.
It disfavours a self-similar fallback-time change; this limits the debris-trigger explanation of the stall.
Period-history models that use the X-ray dip as a clock.
Its archive coverage checks show that no public data cover the 2026 flares; we chose a question that archival data can answer.
Late 2022-2026 flares relative to the published ephemeris; the context of the clock question.
Context: late flares and period-kick models.
Payne et al. 2022 reported that the X-rays decrease during the UV/optical rise; we give the time order and lag.
Huang et al. 2025 reported an X-ray/UV anti-correlation without a lag.
